title: The Case for Shorter Working Weeks
text:
Advocates of a four-day working week argue that productivity need not suffer when employees are given an extra day off. They point to trial programmes in several countries where companies reported lower staff turnover and fewer sick days. Critics, however, question whether these results can be replicated in industries that depend on continuous service, such as healthcare and transport.

The strongest objection, in my view, is not economic but cultural. A shorter week only succeeds if managers abandon the habit of measuring commitment by hours spent at a desk. Until that assumption is challenged, a reduced schedule risks becoming a privilege for a few rather than a change that benefits everyone.

paragraph_translations: People who support a four-day working week argue that output does not have to fall when workers get an extra day off. They refer to trial schemes in several countries, where firms reported that fewer staff left and fewer people took sick leave. Critics, however, doubt that these results would carry over to jobs that require round-the-clock service, such as healthcare and transport.

In my view, the biggest obstacle is cultural rather than financial. A shorter week can only work if managers stop judging how committed someone is by the number of hours they spend at their desk. Until that belief is challenged, a shorter schedule may become an advantage for a small group instead of a change that helps everybody.
